title: Ras to MAPK: From Membrane to Genes

scenes.visual: Title: Ras to MAPK: From Membrane to Genes. Show the membrane-to-nucleus relay as the establishing image.

scenes.tts: A growth factor binds a receptor at the cell surface. Ras switches on, then passes the signal through three kinases: Raf, Mek and Erk. Erk acts on proteins in the cytoplasm and transcription factors in the nucleus. That changes gene expression and cell behaviour. This is how a signal outside reaches the cell’s proteins and genes. Mutations that hold the relay on help drive cancer. So first learn what each step does to the next.

scenes.visual: Begin with a growth factor binding a surface receptor. Trace receptor → Ras-GTP → Raf → MEK → ERK. Branch from ERK to cytoplasmic proteins and nuclear transcription factors, then genes and cell response. Briefly show the relay stuck on beside a cancer label. Keep the complete chain visible as the film’s organising image.

scenes.tts: The active receptor recruits G R B two and S O S. S O S makes Ras release G D P so G T P can bind. Ras is not a kinase. It catches Raf and brings it to the membrane. Binding alone does not open Raf. Contact with membrane lipids and further steps help it open. Two Raf molecules then pair, which is needed for normal activation.
scenes.narration: The active receptor recruits Grb2 and SOS. SOS makes Ras release GDP so GTP can bind. Ras is not a kinase. It catches Raf and brings it to the membrane. Binding alone does not open Raf. Contact with membrane lipids and further steps help it open. Two Raf molecules then pair, which is needed for normal activation.

scenes.visual: Zoom into the active receptor. Grb2 recruits SOS; GDP leaves membrane-anchored Ras and GTP replaces it whole. Ras binds folded Raf and recruits it to the membrane. Show lipid contact and additional opening steps separately from recruitment, then normal Raf pairing and activation.

scenes.tts: Raf adds phosphates to two serines on Mek. Mek adds one to a threonine and one to a tyrosine on Erk. Erk needs both. The narrow relay ends in a wide fan of targets. In the nucleus, Erk phosphorylates Elk one, which helps switch on the immediate early gene c fos.
scenes.narration: Raf adds phosphates to two serines on MEK. MEK adds one to a threonine and one to a tyrosine on ERK. ERK needs both. The narrow relay ends in a wide fan of targets. In the nucleus, ERK phosphorylates Elk-1, which helps switch on the immediate early gene c-fos.
scenes.caption: Raf adds phosphates to two serines on MEK. MEK adds one to a threonine and one to a tyrosine on ERK. ERK needs both. The narrow relay ends in a wide fan of targets. In the nucleus, ERK phosphorylates Elk-1, which helps switch on the immediate early gene c-fos.
scenes.visual: Show Raf phosphorylating two MEK serines, then MEK phosphorylating ERK threonine and tyrosine sites separated by one residue. ERK activates only with both phosphates. Fan out to cytoplasmic targets and a nuclear branch: ERK → Elk-1 → c-fos. Distinguish phosphorylation arrows from gene activation.

scenes.tts: In cancer, mutations can hold Ras or Raf on. B Raf V six hundred E can signal without Ras G T P. A Raf inhibitor can block it. But with normal B Raf and active Ras, drug-bound Raf can activate a drug-free partner. Erk activity then rises. A Mek inhibitor holds Mek inactive below Raf. The drug’s effect depends on the pathway’s state.
scenes.narration: In cancer, mutations can hold Ras or Raf on. B-Raf V600E can signal without Ras-GTP. A Raf inhibitor can block it. But with normal B-Raf and active Ras, drug-bound Raf can activate a drug-free partner. ERK activity then rises. A MEK inhibitor holds MEK inactive below Raf. The drug’s effect depends on the pathway’s state.

scenes.visual: Compare two labelled contexts. B-Raf V600E signals without Ras-GTP; a Raf inhibitor blocks downstream signalling. Omit mutant partner state. With normal B-Raf and active Ras, show a paired Raf complex: drug-bound Raf activates its drug-free partner and MEK–ERK output rises. Add a MEK inhibitor below Raf, holding MEK inactive and blocking output.

scenes.tts: The relay also limits itself. Erk weakens S O S and Raf by phosphorylation. It turns on genes for phosphatases that remove Erk’s activating phosphates. That takes longer, because a protein must be made. Signal duration also depends on the stimulus, cell type and dose. Timing helps shape the response.

scenes.visual: Show fast inhibitory phosphorylation arrows from ERK to SOS and Raf. Separately show ERK-induced phosphatase gene expression, a protein-production delay, then removal of ERK phosphates. Label stimulus, cell type and dose beside a duration window; avoid a universal timing-to-fate rule.

scenes.tts: Three kinase tiers give amplification and separate control points. Other MAP kinase pathways use the same plan with different kinases. Scaffolds hold a module’s kinases together, helping them signal mainly to each other. They also help decide where the cascade runs.

scenes.visual: Show three kinase tiers with amplification and a control point at each tier. Place a generic second module alongside it using different kinase blocks. Scaffold brackets keep each module together; show a location marker to explain that scaffolds also position the cascade.

scenes.tts: Milder over-activation also matters. Mutations inherited or new at conception cause developmental syndromes called Ras opathies. Their effects differ between tissues. The relay carries the signal, but its control and the cell’s context shape the answer.

scenes.visual: Show mild pathway over-activation associated with developmental effects in face, heart and growth. Label RASopathies and mutations inherited or new at conception. End on the complete receptor-to-genes relay, with feedback and scaffold controls visible.
Hold the full relay and its cytoplasmic and nuclear outputs for the closing frame.
